lessons.title: Claiming HRA and Home Loan Benefits Together

body.text: HRA and home loan benefits come from different parts of the tax law, and nothing forces you to choose between them. What decides whether you get both is simple: the home you rent must be the one you live in, and the home you own must be somewhere you do not.

children.text: "You have a home loan, so you can't claim HRA." Salaried Indians hear this from colleagues, relatives and sometimes even payroll teams. It is wrong. An engineer who owns a flat in Nagpur and rents in Hyderabad for work, or a banker who bought in Pune and moved to Mumbai, can legitimately claim both. The trouble starts when both homes are in the same city, or when people misunderstand how each benefit works.
Two Benefits, Two Parts of the Law

body.caption: Home-related tax benefits for a salaried individual, tax year 2026-27

body.text: HRA reduces your salary income. Home loan interest reduces your income from house property. Principal repayment sits inside the ₹1,50,000 deduction pool. Because they work on different heads and limits, one does not cancel the other. All of them, however, need the old regime.

cells: You own a flat in your hometown, where your parents live, and rent in the city where you work
Keep proof that you live and work in the other city
You own a flat in another city and have let it out, and rent where you work
Full interest against the rent received. A net loss reduces other income by up to ₹2,00,000
The rent you receive is taxable income from house property
You own a flat in the same city where you rent
Possible, but likely to be questioned
Depends on whether your flat is let out or kept for your use
Document genuine reasons: the flat is let out, too small, too far from work or not ready
You live in the flat you own
Tell your employer so HRA is not exempted in your TDS

body.title: Quick Check: Both or One?
body.question: Ishaan works for a consulting firm in Gurugram and rents a flat there. He owns a flat in Jaipur with a home loan, which stays locked while his family visits occasionally. He is on the old regime. What can he claim?
options: Only HRA, because he cannot claim two housing benefits
Only home loan interest, because owning a home disqualifies HRA
Both: HRA for the Gurugram rent and up to ₹2,00,000 of interest on the Jaipur flat
Neither, because the Jaipur flat is empty
body.explanation: Ishaan lives in a rented home in Gurugram that he does not own, so he passes the HRA tests. His Jaipur flat is not let out, so it is treated as self-occupied and he can deduct up to ₹2,00,000 of interest. The two benefits are independent.

children.text: Worked Example: When the Combination Tips the Regime

Rahul works for a bank in Hyderabad on a gross salary of ₹24,00,000, with basic ₹1,00,000 and HRA ₹50,000 a month. He rents in Madhapur for ₹45,000 a month. He also owns a flat in Nagpur, where his parents live, with a home loan on which he pays ₹2,60,000 of interest a year. His own PF contribution of ₹1,44,000 plus a small life insurance premium already fill the ₹1,50,000 limit under Section 123 (80C), and he claims ₹25,000 for health insurance and ₹50,000 for NPS.

His exempt HRA is the smallest of ₹6,00,000, ₹5,40,000 minus ₹1,20,000 = ₹4,20,000, and ₹6,00,000, which is ₹4,20,000. His home loan interest deduction is capped at ₹2,00,000, even though he paid ₹2,60,000.

body.text: Notice that Rahul's principal repayment adds nothing, because his PF already fills the ₹1,50,000 limit, and ₹60,000 of his interest is lost above the ₹2,00,000 cap. Always count only the amounts that actually reduce your income, not everything you pay the bank.

children.text: When the Owned Home Is Let Out

Priya rents a flat in Bengaluru for work and has let out her own flat in Wakad, Pune for ₹20,000 a month. She pays ₹10,000 a year in property tax and ₹3,50,000 of home loan interest. Her HRA claim for the Bengaluru flat is unaffected. The Pune flat creates a separate calculation.

body.title: Priya's ₹1,89,000 house property loss under each regime

columns.label: Old regime
points: Loss of ₹1,89,000 is within the ₹2,00,000 cap
The whole loss is set off against her salary under Section 109
At a 30% slab, that saves about ₹58,968
Any loss above ₹2,00,000 would carry forward for 8 years

columns.label: New regime
points: Interest is allowed only up to the rent income after the 30% deduction
Her house property income becomes nil, and the ₹1,89,000 loss is simply lost
No set-off against salary and no carry forward
HRA for the Bengaluru flat is also not allowed

body.title: For the curious: a home loan on a flat that is still under construction

children.text: Many buyers keep renting while their flat is being built. HRA is unaffected, since you still pay rent for the home you live in. Interest paid before construction is complete cannot be deducted in those years. Instead, the total pre-construction interest is claimed in five equal instalments starting from the year construction is completed, alongside that year's interest. For a self-occupied home, the instalment and current interest together stay within the ₹2,00,000 cap.

body.title: Try It: Sameer's Let-Out Flat
body.prompt: Sameer rents in Mumbai for work and has let out his flat in Nashik for ₹15,000 a month. He pays ₹6,000 a year in property tax and ₹3,20,000 a year in home loan interest. Under the old regime, what is his loss from house property for the year? Enter the loss as a positive number in rupees.
body.explanation: Annual rent ₹1,80,000 minus property tax ₹6,000 is ₹1,74,000. The 30% standard deduction is ₹52,200, leaving ₹1,21,800. Subtracting interest of ₹3,20,000 gives a loss of ₹1,98,200. It is within the ₹2,00,000 cap, so under the old regime the full loss can be set off against his salary. His HRA claim for the Mumbai flat is separate and unaffected.

body.title: Scenario: Two Homes in One City
body.scenario: Anjali owns a 1BHK in Andheri West, bought before her marriage, with a home loan. She has let it out for ₹35,000 a month. She now lives with her husband and two children in a rented 3BHK in Powai at ₹75,000 a month, closer to the children's school and her office. She claims HRA on the Powai rent and deducts the home loan interest on Andheri against the rent she receives.
body.prompt: Is this allowed? What might a tax officer ask, and how should Anjali prepare?
body.modelAnswer: Yes, both claims can be valid. The HRA tests look at the home she lives in, the Powai flat, which she rents and does not own. Her Andheri flat is let out, so its rent is taxable and the interest is deductible against it under the let-out rules. Because both homes are in Mumbai, an officer may ask why she rents while owning a flat in the same city. Her answer is strong if it is documented: the owned flat is a 1BHK that cannot house a family of four, it is let out to a tenant under a registered agreement, the rent is declared in her return, and Powai is near her office and the school. She should keep both rent agreements, bank records of rent paid and received, the tenant's details and her children's school address. The arrangement looks suspicious only if the Andheri flat is not really let out, or if the family actually lives there.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Self-Occupied Cap
body.textWithBlank: Under the old regime, interest on a loan for a self-occupied home is deductible up to ₹___ lakh a year under Section 22(2) of the Income-tax Act, 2025.
body.explanation: The limit is ₹2,00,000 a year, unchanged since 2014. It corresponds to Section 24(b) of the 1961 Act and is not available under the new regime.

body.title: Claiming HRA and a Home Loan Together
steps: Confirm the home you rent is the one you live in, and the home you own is in a different city or let out
Get the interest certificate from your lender, split into interest and principal, for the tax year
Declare both the rent and the home loan interest to your employer in Form 124, with lender and landlord details
If your own flat is let out, keep the rent agreement and declare the rent received as income from house property
Check whether your principal repayment actually adds to your 80C deduction or is already covered by PF and other investments
Compare old regime tax with both benefits against new regime tax before choosing your regime

cards.definition: The Income-tax Act, 2025 provision allowing deduction of interest on a home loan against house property income. Corresponds to Section 24(b) of the 1961 Act.
A home you own and live in, or that is not let out, such as a hometown flat used by your family. Interest deduction is capped at ₹2,00,000 under the old regime.
A home you own and rent to a tenant. Rent is taxable, and interest is fully deductible against it, but the net loss can reduce other income by only ₹2,00,000 under Section 109.
Carries forward unabsorbed house property losses for 8 years, set off only against future house property income. Corresponds to Section 71B.
The Income-tax Act, 2025 deduction that includes home loan principal repayment within ₹1,50,000. Corresponds to Section 80C.
Interest paid before a home is completed, claimed in five equal instalments from the year of completion.

points: HRA exemption and home loan benefits work on different heads and can be claimed together under the old regime
Rent where you live and own somewhere else: the classic case is a hometown flat plus a rented flat in your work city
Self-occupied home loan interest is capped at ₹2,00,000 a year under Section 22(2), and principal counts only within the ₹1,50,000 limit
For a let-out home, rent is taxable and the net loss reduces other income by up to ₹2,00,000, with the rest carried forward for 8 years
Owning and renting in the same city is not banned but invites questions, so document genuine reasons
The combination of HRA and home loan interest is often what makes the old regime cheaper than the new one
